summary:
Georgia stands under the national framework of the United States; the federal document, entry and screening rules set out in the national record apply in this state without modification. The state-specific layer adds three things a trans visitor should weigh: documented street violence concentrated in Atlanta, a statutory ban on gender-affirming care for minors, and a measurable contraction of adult surgical care under federal funding pressure.

Violence is the sharpest documented risk. In April 2023 the Atlanta Police Department said it was actively investigating three violent crimes against transgender women in the city that year, following the fatal shootings of two Black transgender women a week apart. A January 2023 shooting that left a transgender woman in critical condition also remained open at that point. The department publicly acknowledged the epidemic-level violence that Black and Brown transgender women face in the United States. The incidents are Atlanta's, and Atlanta is one city in the state, but it is the state's largest urban centre and the point at which the available record concentrates.

The recorded killing rate for trans women in Georgia is 4.8 per 100,000 per year. That figure is an acknowledged floor drawn from a monitoring project known to undercount, so the true rate is at least this and probably higher; it should be read as a minimum exposure level rather than a measured ceiling.

Care access is restricted by state law. Governor Brian Kemp signed Senate Bill 140 on 23 March 2023, barring licensed medical professionals from providing hormone therapy or gender-transition surgery to patients under 18, with licence revocation available as a penalty. The ban took effect on 1 July 2023. Minors who had begun hormone replacement therapy before that date may continue under the law. The ACLU of Georgia said at the time of signing that it would sue.

Adult care has also narrowed in practice. On 13 February 2025 Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah cancelled all gender-affirming surgeries, including a pre-approved double mastectomy for a 24-year-old transgender man, citing a responsibility to follow state and federal laws and regulations. The Savannah Pride Center reported that at least two other area residents were denied care in the same period. A trans adult seeking surgical care in Georgia should therefore expect providers to test each case against current funding rules before scheduling.
tangentialFactors:
Georgia's two care-related positions sit awkwardly together. Senate Bill 140 prohibits gender-transition treatment for minors inside the state, while the State Health Benefit Plan, after a settlement reached in October 2023 in federal court in Atlanta, can be required to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for the minors of its members even when that care is delivered outside Georgia. The state thus bars the treatment locally while its own insurance plan may fund it elsewhere.

The February 2025 cancellation at Memorial Health in Savannah was justified by the hospital in terms of state and federal law and regulation, an explanation that appears to reference the federal executive order of 28 January 2025 denying Medicare and Medicaid funding to providers of youth gender-transition care. The practical effect reached an adult patient, which indicates that federal funding pressure is reshaping adult surgical provision in Georgia as well as care for minors.

The violence record and the care record come from different periods and different sources: the Atlanta shootings and police response date from 2023, the killing-rate figure is an annualised estimate from an undercounted monitor, and the care closures run from 2023 to 2025. They are not a single trend line, and none of the sources ranks Georgia against other states on any of these measures.
localsOnly:
Georgia's public-employee health coverage is the one area where the state's position moved in the opposite direction to its statute. A lawsuit filed in December 2022 argued that the State Health Benefit Plan discriminated illegally by refusing to pay for gender-affirming care, and in October 2023 plaintiffs announced a settlement in federal court in Atlanta requiring the plan to pay for medically necessary gender-affirming care for employees, their spouses and their dependents. Coverage for state employees therefore continued by settlement even after Senate Bill 140 took effect on 1 July 2023.

For residents and providers, Senate Bill 140 is a licensing matter as well as a treatment restriction: a clinician who provides hormone therapy or transition surgery to a patient under 18 faces possible revocation of their licence, subject to the exception for minors already on hormone replacement therapy before 1 July 2023. The ACLU of Georgia announced an intention to sue after the bill was signed; the inventory does not record the outcome of any such action.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the ACLU of Georgia filed and how it fared on any challenge to Senate Bill 140 is unresolved in the sources held here; only the announcement of an intention to sue is recorded.

The disposition of the three Atlanta investigations opened in 2023 is unresolved: the sources do not say whether arrests, charges or convictions followed, nor whether the January 2023 shooting was solved.

Whether the Memorial Health University Medical Center cancellation of 13 February 2025 is permanent, partial or subsequently reversed is not sourced. The same is true of the reported denials of care to other Savannah-area residents.

The State Health Benefit Plan settlement is recorded as announced in October 2023; whether its terms remain in force, were modified, or are subject to further litigation is not sourced here.

No region-specific information is held in this inventory on Georgia's rules for changing a gender marker on a state driver's licence or birth certificate, on any state facility or restroom restriction, on hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, or on partner recognition. Those questions remain unresolved at the state level and are not answered by the national record.
